transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-25
Start: 14:30 PST
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood Runtime Eng), Mark Holloway (Vela Eng Mgr), Ana Ruiz (Vela SRE), Li Chen (Vela ML Infra), Diego Ramos (Vela Data Sci)

Summary:
High-level: deep dive into TokenStore / KV layer behavior under Vela's workload: high prefix reuse across concurrent sessions, periodic bursts causing paging, and questions about eviction policy and graceful fallback to smaller models or disk spill. Action items and benchmarking plan agreed.

Topics discussed:
- TokenStore prefix affinity and hot-prefix detection
- Eviction patterns: time-based vs recency vs per-prefix quotas
- Paging/spill behavior and impact on latency tail
- Long-context sessions (50k+ tokens) and KV retention strategy
- Prefetch heuristics and batching interplay
- Fallback routing to smaller/quantized variants under pressure
- Observability: telemetry points and dashboards to collect

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone, um thanks for taking the deep dive today. we wanna get into the tokenstore findings you sent and, uh, sort of map to runtime fixes and mitigation plans. i think priya's going to kick off with some notes?
[00:28] Priya: yeah sure, thanks. quick context — from the traces you shared, we see very high prefix reuse across many sessions, like the same intro prompt hitting the model thousands of times per hour, which is great for cache hit rate in ideal world, but youre seeing weird eviction cascades when a burst comes in.
[00:55] Mark: correct, those bursts line up with our nightly enrichment job and also some user-initiated batching, so sometimes we go from 500 qps to 3k qps for 30s. latency tails spike and the tokenstore starts paging.
[01:22] Jordan: when you say paging, just to align terms, we're talking about the KV layer spilling older prefix entries to local SSD or host memory pages being reclaimed, right? not some DB call.
[01:39] Ana: yeah it's host memory reclaiming and then spike creates pressure and the runtime drops older prefixes, i think. some nodes show higher swap IO.
[01:52] Priya: based on the dump, eviction looks like a combined recency + size heuristic — we observed larger prefix trees (like long conversation histories) being evicted first because they consume more slots and push smaller but hotter prefixes out.
[02:15] Samir: that's not ideal for prefix affinity, because small hot prefixes are used repeatedly. so what we're seeing is the classic hot-objects eviction paradox.
[02:30] Li: to add, our sessions have long trailing context — some customers keep histories of 40k tokens and re-send prefixes for personalization, which makes some prefixes large and seldom reused but expensive.
[02:47] Priya: yeah, two high-level knobs we think will help: per-prefix soft quotas and age-weighted admission (so huge prefixes are admitted more conservatively), and proactive prefetch for prefixes identified as 'hot' by frequency counters.
[03:12] Mark: can you explain per-prefix soft quota? how'd that work in practice?
[03:21] Priya: imagine you assign a budget of tokenstore entries per prefix key; if a prefix grows beyond budget, eviction for that prefix is prioritized or older vectors compacted. it's not a hard deny, but it avoids one big prefix evicting lots of small ones.
[03:45] Diego: any risk of breaking session semantics? some of our app logic expects the full context (like persona info).
[03:55] Jordan: good question — we can tier the retention: essential metadata + summary embedding kept always; raw long tail vectors can be elided or compressed with lossy quantization. that's where tradeoffs with quantization come in — more aggressive quantization reduces memory but can hurt generation quality.
[04:20] Samir: also there's an autoscaling path: when tokenstore pressure crosses X%, we can spin up temporary dedicated pool nodes and route hot prefixes there, so the eviction pressure stays localized. that is more expensive but keeps latency SLO.
[04:43] Ana: do we have a graceful fallback policy? sometimes the app prefers increased latency over degraded quality.
[04:51] Priya: we support policy chaining: fallback to smaller quantized model (lower memory), fallback to dedicated pool, or fallback to concurrency limiting with queueing+priority. order of fallback is configurable per-customer.
[05:10] Mark: we saw a case where fallback to a quantized variant increased hallucinations slightly, which is risky for our domain. we prefer spinning up capacity if possible.
[05:23] Samir: understood — so immediate mitigation in short term: prioritize hot prefixes, tweak eviction to per-prefix quotas, and add a prefetch window around active sessions. medium term: test autoscale/dedicated fallback during synthetic bursts.

[05:50] [10 minute mark summary by Priya; notes slightly garbled] Priya: telemetry — collect per-prefix hit-rate, size, last-used-ts, admission-count, eviction-reason, node mem pressure. we wanna see prefix-affinity heatmaps. also, add a synthetic workload that imitates your enrichment bursts.
[06:21] Li: we've got an internal tool that can produce the enrichment pattern and also surface specific session ids. i'll send those.

[06:40] [07:00] Diego: also i think the prefix keys may not be normalized at ingestion — sometimes the same logical prefix has tiny token differences, leading to low reuse. could canonicalization help?
[07:15] Priya: definitely. simple normalization or fingerprinting reduces prefix cardinality and improves reuse. but be careful — you dont want to over-normalize and lose personalization signals.
[07:34] Mark: we already strip whitespace and do light canonicalization but not semantic hashing. maybe that'd help.

[07:50] Jordan: i wanna dig into the eviction algorithm we run by default — it's kind of an approximate LRU with size weighting and a small random sample to avoid pathological scans. downside is it doesn't respect prefix ownership. adding prefix quotas requires tracking a small counter per prefix and accounting when admitting new slots. cost is a few extra bytes per prefix and an extra eviction pass when threshold reached.
[08:24] Ana: how much extra CPU does the accounting add? our nodes are already 60-70% CPU on bursts.
[08:32] Jordan: small — most cost is memory writes for counters and an occasional scan; we measured <5% throughput regression in similar workloads, but that depends. can run with accounting in read-only for a while to collect telemetry before flipping enforcement.

[08:52] [09:15] Mark: what's the recommended TTL for these prefixes? we tried 24h and still saw growth.
[09:24] Priya: TTLs depend on usage patterns; for your workload with nightly enrichment, shorter TTL for large prefixes (e.g., 6-12h) plus an LRU for small prefixes helps. Another option: size-based TTL scaling — bigger prefixes get smaller TTLs.
[09:46] Li: hmm ok. also, can prefetched entries be evicted earlier? like a lower residency for prefetched vs actively used keys?
[09:58] Priya: yes, label them as warm-pool entries with lower priority. if access pattern hits them frequently we promote them to hot.

[10:15] Samir: let's talk about paging to disk. currently runtime spills to local SSD when mem pressure is high — that introduces ~50-200ms tail spikes depending on IO. any constraints on Vela side for local disk?
[10:33] Ana: our policy disallows persistent local storage on some clusters, so we prefer in-memory but can accept short-lived disk if slow. but we worry about IO noise from other processes.
[10:44] Jordan: for on-prem we recommend isolated NVMe or ramdisk where possible; in VPC you'd want dedicated instance local NVMe or move to ram-backed caches. Another approach is to avoid spill by proactive admission and spin up dedicated pool before spilling.

[11:05] Mark: you mentioned prefetch heuristics — how aggressive are you suggesting for prefetch window? we worry about loading a lot of cold data.
[11:15] Priya: prefetch should be frequency-based: only prefetch for prefixes with recent high re-hit probability, and limit to N prefixes per session. heuristics can be tuned via a EWMA of access rate and a confidence threshold. default we use a 2-5 prefix lookahead and a soft budget.
[11:40] Diego: is there telemetry to see if prefetch pays off? we need to know hit-rate delta vs extra memory.
[11:48] Priya: yes — prefetch hit delta, prefetch evictions, and prefetch memory footprint are the core metrics. we'll add these to the dashboard.

[12:05] [12:30] Mark: ok can you show an example of the fallback policy config? like if mem>85% then route to dedicated pool else quantized fallback?
[12:43] Samir: sure we have a YAML example — but verbally: threshold triggers: mem>85% -> try dedicated pool spin-up (if capacity allowed), else mem>92% -> throttle new sessions and apply quantized variant for low-priority traffic, and mem>98% -> emergency queueing + reject lowest priority.
[13:05] Ana: we need a mode where we choose higher latency over lower quality. can you configure priority by route?
[13:12] Priya: yes route-level policies exist — you can set route X to prefer capacity fallback, route Y to prefer quantized model.

[13:30] Jordan: small gotcha — switching model variants mid-session requires careful KV translation if KV formats differ. we do a lightweight transform for compressed representations but it's not zero-cost.
[13:45] Li: what's the impact on latency when transforming KV entries for variant change?
[13:52] Jordan: depends on size; usually a few ms per prefix, but bulk transforms during big changes can add tens to hundreds of ms. can be mitigated by incremental transform and lazy migration.

[14:10] [14:40] Diego: do you have recommendations for quantization levels that are least likely to degrade our use-case? we use factual QA a lot.
[14:50] Priya: for QA heavy tasks, 4-bit quant with per-channel scales tends to be ok for many models but you must validate on your eval set. we often recommend running a small eval with the quantized variant; if QA F1 drops beyond threshold then prefer capacity-based fallback.

[15:10] Mark: we wanted to run a POC on dedicated nodes. how long to provision?
[15:17] Samir: for Hosted Dedicated within Redwood, provisioning is automated — typically a few minutes for soft capacity and a few hours for reserved capacity depending on region. for private on-prem it depends on infra but we can provide an image to bootstrap.
[15:32] Ana: our security team will want SAML + KMS integration details for private nodes.
[15:38] Priya: we'll share the security docs and an on-prem checklist.

[15:55] [16:10] Mark: curious about metrics we should collect from our side — what logs/trace points to capture?
[16:18] Priya: per-request tokenstore hit boolean, per-request prefixes touched, prefix sizes, eviction_reason, node mem usage, GC/compaction events, and per-model latency breakdown pre/post KV. also important: percent time spent in KV lookup vs generation.
[16:40] Li: ok we'll add instrumentation to surface these in our monitoring.
end_note: Call ended with agreement on synthetic benchmark and dashboard sharing. Follow-up scheduled.
